subject: botany

unit.name: Ecological Adaptations, Succession and Ecological Services (Botany)

chapter: Ecological Adaptations, Succession and Ecological Services
question_text: Give in detail the anatomical adaptations shown by xerophytes.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section, Chapter 13, book p.36, SAQ 6. All five of the book's points are kept and grouped into four marked blocks; the sclerenchymatous hypodermis, the compact mesophyll and the water-storing parenchyma of succulents are added from standard texts. Note on the book's wording: it writes 'Stomata are hypostomatous', which is loose — a LEAF is hypostomatous, a stoma is not. The card says the leaves are hypostomatous. Only one source book is held for botany — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand is physics-only and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card, not merely unrun. The 1+1+1+1 split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Ecological Adaptations, Succession and Ecological Services · 4 marks

steps.label: Cuticle and epidermis
lines: A thick cuticle is present on the
epidermis, and it reduces water loss through
the surface.
The epidermis itself may be multilayered
(multiple epidermis).
Below it a hypodermis of sclerenchyma is
often present.
steps.why: Water leaves the plant through the surface, so the surface is thickened in three layers one after another: cuticle outside, several rows of epidermis under it, then a sclerenchymatous hypodermis.
common_mistakes: Writing that the cuticle is thin or absent. That is a hydrophyte feature.
Confusing hypodermis with hypocotyl. The hypodermis is the layer under the epidermis.
steps.memory_tip: Three layers from outside in: cuticle, multiple epidermis, sclerenchyma hypodermis.
steps.margin_note: Four tissue blocks for four marks. Give the reason with each one.

steps.label: Stomata
lines: Leaves are hypostomatous: the stomata lie
on the lower surface only, away from
direct sunlight.
The stomata are sunken — each one sits in a
pit below the surface, often lined with
hairs.
The pit holds still, moist air, so less
water diffuses out.
steps.why: Water vapour diffuses out fastest into dry moving air. A sunken stoma opens into a small pocket of still, humid air, which slows the diffusion at the point where it happens.
common_mistakes: Writing epistomatous. Epi means upper and belongs to floating leaves, not xerophytes.
Saying stomata are absent. They are present, but sunken and fewer.
steps.memory_tip: Down and in: down to the lower surface, in to a sunken pit.
steps.margin_note: This block usually carries the mark. Write hypostomatous AND sunken.

steps.label: Mechanical tissue
lines: Mechanical tissue is very well developed.
Sclerenchyma and collenchyma occur in large
amounts in the stem and the leaf.
They hold the shape of the plant even when
the cells lose water, so the plant does not
collapse during drought.
steps.why: A hydrophyte is supported by the water around it; a xerophyte has nothing but its own tissue, and it must stay upright even when its cells are short of water.
common_mistakes: Writing that mechanical tissue is poorly developed. That is the hydrophyte answer.
Naming only sclerenchyma without saying what it does here.
steps.memory_tip: Hydrophyte: poorly developed. Xerophyte: very well developed. Same tissue, opposite answers.
steps.margin_note: One line of fact and one of reason. Do not expand this block.

steps.label: Vascular tissue and mesophyll

lines.text: Vascular tissue, especially xylem, is well

lines: Water reaching the deep root has a long way
to travel, so wide, plentiful xylem is
needed.
Mesophyll is compact with few air spaces,
and succulents add a water-storing
parenchyma.
steps.why: The xylem is the exact opposite of the hydrophyte case: here water is absorbed at one point far below the ground and has to be carried the whole length of the plant, so the conducting tissue is enlarged.
common_mistakes: Writing that xylem is reduced. Reduced xylem is the hydrophyte answer.
Leaving out the mesophyll. Compact mesophyll with few air spaces is a marked point.
steps.memory_tip: Long distance to carry the water, so wide xylem. Xerophyte xylem is well developed; hydrophyte xylem is not.
steps.margin_note: End here. The xylem contrast is the line an examiner looks for last.

insider_note: Anatomical means internal tissue, so spines and deep roots earn nothing here. The safest four blocks are cuticle and epidermis, sunken stomata, mechanical tissue, xylem — and every one of them is the exact opposite of the hydrophyte answer.
